title: In Seven States, Voters Side with Direct Democracy
author: Pascal Sabino
content:
Voters in seven states resoundingly affirmed their power to pass laws without
going through their lawmakers on Tuesday, approving ballot measures that will
protect future citizen-led ballot initiatives and rejecting efforts to
restrict them.

In California, North Dakota, South Dakota, Utah, voters were deciding whether
to require 60-percent supermajorities to pass some constitutional amendments.
In Idaho, lawmakers asked them to ban all future initiatives on drug policy.

All of these measures lost decisively, by margins ranging from 13 percentage
points in North Dakota to 33 points in Idaho. For direct democracy advocates,
these decisive results reflect voter disdain towards efforts to restrain their
power. “The thread through all of these states is that politicians were trying
to take rights away from voters at an epic scale,” says Hannah Ledford,
executive director of the Fairness Project, a national organization that helps
organize progressive measures. “Overwhelmingly, voters said ‘No way.’”

In Missouri and Montana, two states where Republican officials have tried to
derail popular initiatives with new restrictions and litigation, organizers
collected hundreds of thousands of signatures to put measures on the ballot
that would [enshrine a fundamental right to direct
democracy](https://boltsmag.org/missouri-and-montana-measures-aim-to-protect-
direct-democracy/).

Those proposals easily prevailed and will hinder state officials from cracking
down on future campaigns. Legal experts told _Bolts_ that the measures will
give Missouri and Montana some of the strongest legal protections for ballot
initiatives in the nation.

These results come in the wake of years of attacks on direct democracy,
largely in GOP-run states where lawmakers have responded to progressive
measures on abortion rights and Medicaid expansion with a
[barrage](https://boltsmag.org/oklahoma-restricts-ballot-initiative-process/)
of new rules [making it harder](https://boltsmag.org/florida-new-restrictions-
on-ballot-initiative-process/) for citizens to get measures on the ballot. But
these restrictions typically fare poorly whenever lawmakers have to put them
to a vote—as they did again on Tuesday.

### **Missouri and Montana**

Advocates in these states grew frustrated in recent years at what they called
the GOP’s “thousand cuts strategy” by lawmakers to limit citizen initiatives,
as [_Bolts_ as previously reported](https://boltsmag.org/missouri-and-montana-
measures-aim-to-protect-direct-democracy/)—including legislation sponsored by
GOP lawmakers to create onerous new requirements for putting measures on the
ballot and maneuvers by state officials to derail citizen-led campaigns.

Both states’ supreme courts have repeatedly stepped in to rebuke GOP
interference, but advocates worried about courts becoming less favorable to
them.

So this year, they went on the offensive by sponsoring constitutional
amendments to affirm that the people have a fundamental right to direct
democracy. On Tuesday, Missourians approved Amendment 6 by a margin of 20
percentage points. Montanans approved Initiative 133 by a margin of 30
percentage points.

Voters “sent a very clear message to their legislatures that this right is
protected and cannot be taken away,” said Ledford, whose organization helped
expand Medicaid via ballot initiatives in both Missouri and Montana.

Legal experts say codifying this right will help prevent state officials from
putting a thumb on the scale against initiatives they don’t like, and it will
give organizers a stronger legal tool to challenge laws that make it harder
for citizens to circulate petitions to get a measure on the ballot and pass
initiatives.

The amendments instruct the courts to use a high legal standard known as
strict scrutiny when reviewing hurdles to initiative campaigns. “If something
impacts a fundamental right, courts are supposed to basically subject it to
very rigorous questioning,” Derek Clinger, a scholar at the University of
Wisconsin Law School, [told _Bolts_ last month](https://boltsmag.org/missouri-
and-montana-measures-aim-to-protect-direct-democracy).

Missouri and Montana are the first to add such a right explicitly in their
constitutions, though courts in other states like Idaho and Utah have
recognized similar protections.

![](https://boltsmag.org/wp-
content/uploads/2026/09/image_from_ios_1024.jpg)Organizers for CI-133, the
initiative to strengthen initiatives in Montana (photo courtesy Montanans
Decide)

Both measures also contain more specific safeguards, geared to protect ballot
initiatives from the sort of attacks they’ve faced in each state. Montana’s
amendment lays out a clear timeline for courts to resolve legal disputes over
petitions so that state officials cannot use lawsuits to make initiative
campaigns miss their filing deadlines.

Missouri’s makes it harder for legislators to roll back popular initiatives,
requiring lawmakers to muster an 80 percent-supermajority to amend a measure
that voters have approved or to [double down on a law voters have
rejected](https://boltsmag.org/missourians-veto-new-gerrymander-and-make-it-
trickier-for-gop-to-adopt-another/). It also bans state officials from putting
biased language into the descriptions of measures on the ballot. Tuesday’s
ballot included a GOP-sponsored amendment to repeal an abortion rights measure
that voters enacted in 2024; Missourians rejected that effort by 10 points.

Chris Melody Fields Figueredo, executive director of Ballot Initiative
Strategy Center, predicts that other states will follow Missouri and Montana’s
example, telling _Bolts_ , _“_ I think we are going to see more attempts to
ensure that direct democracy remains in the hands of the people and free from
government interference.”

### **North Dakota and South Dakota**

Republican legislators in the Dakotas proposed very similar measures that
would have required voters to muster a 60-percent supermajority to approve any
future constitutional amendments.

Voters soundly rejected both proposals, by 14 percentage points in North
Dakota and 16 points in South Dakota.

Had these measures been in place, some of the Dakotas’ emblematic recent
citizen-led initiatives would have failed. North Dakotans approved a measure
in
[2018](https://ballotpedia.org/North_Dakota_Measure_1,_Ethics_Commission,_Foreign_Political_Contribution_Ban,_and_Conflicts_of_Interest_Initiative_\(2018\))
to set up an ethics commission with 54 percent of the vote, and South Dakotans
in
[2022](https://ballotpedia.org/South_Dakota_Constitutional_Amendment_D,_Medicaid_Expansion_Initiative_\(2022\))
expanded Medicaid eligibility to cover more than 50,000 residents with 56
percent of the vote.

Resentful at these citizen-led maneuvers, Republican lawmakers have already
tried several times to constrain their powers. But voters have repeatedly
opposed these attempts; they rejected a proposed North Dakota ban on
initiatives that would spend public funds, and two prior proposals to require
a supermajority in South Dakota.

The most recent effort was in 2022, when the GOP [rushed a summer
election](https://boltsmag.org/amendment-c-south-dakota-medicaid/) in a failed
attempt to change the rules ahead of the fall referendum that expanded
Medicaid.

“I don’t know if they will ever give it up, trying to make it harder to use
direct engagement by the citizens to petition the government,” said Rick
Weiland, co-chair of Dakotans for Health, a grassroots network that campaigned
for Medicaid expansion. “But this is the third time at the altar, and they
were resoundingly rejected.”

![](https://boltsmag.org/wp-
content/uploads/2026/07/471192472_1008530447968950_8549873797342003467_n-e1784131141481.jpg)An
organizer in South Dakota assists with efforts to collect citizen petitions
(photo via Dakotans for Health/Facebook).  

[Anti-abortion groups and
politicians](https://northdakotamonitor.com/2026/10/23/some-measure-1-backers-
see-it-as-a-roadblock-to-potential-abortion-rights-initiatives-in-nd/) touted
the supermajority requirement as a way to prevent future abortion rights
initiatives, and Tuesday’s results mean future citizen measures to legalize
abortion in the Dakotas remain plausible. A 2024 effort
[failed](https://www.nytimes.com/interactive/2024/11/05/us/elections/results-
south-dakota-amendment-g-right-to-abortion.html) at the ballot box in South
Dakota, while a similar measure in North Dakota failed to qualify.

“To get abortion rights back in South Dakota, you’re never going to get it
done through the legislature—your best shot is to do it through an initiated
amendment,” said Weiland, whose organization also ran the 2024 measure for
abortion access. “So I think the door is open.”

### **California and Utah**

These two states are poised to reject narrower measures that would have
required a supermajority to approve new tax-related initiatives.

The Utah measure, Amendment B, would have required support from 60 percent of
voters for citizen initiatives that raise taxes. Under that higher standard,
the Medicaid expansion Utah voters passed in 2018 with 53 percent of the vote
would have failed, since it was funded by a sales tax increase.

Voters rejected Amendment B by almost 25 points.

![](https://boltsmag.org/wp-
content/uploads/2026/11/16126055619097-2400x1462.jpg)A signature gatherer
discusses a petition to legalize marijuana in Sacramento, California, in 2016.
Californians ended up legalizing marijuana that fall. (AP Photo/Rich
Pedroncelli)

California’s Proposition 43 would have required that ballot measures win two-
thirds support to create a special local tax, such as the so-called [mansion
tax](https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2022-11-12/lopez-column-
citizens-led-the-way-on-la-homelessness-tax-measure) passed in Los Angeles in
2022.

It was placed on the ballot by the Democratic legislature [as part of a deal
with a conservative advocacy group](https://www.sacbee.com/news/politics-
government/capitol-alert/article316274423.html) that was gearing up to place a
much more aggressive proposal on the ballot; theirs would have applied
retroactively, repealing past tax measures, like the mansion tax, that fell
short of a supermajority. The conservative group agreed to drop their own
effort if lawmakers advanced the compromise version.

Proposition 43’s sponsor, Democratic Assemblymember Buffy Wicks, then urged
Californians to reject it. The California Democratic Party [also called on
voters](https://cadem.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/FINAL-2026-General-
Election-Endorsements.pdf) to reject the amendment.

The measure is trailing 57 to 43, though the margin may still change as the
count is continuing in this state.

California, however, may still see a rare instance this cycle where some
voters make it harder to pass initiatives—though at the local level.

San Francisco officials put forward a charter amendment to quadruple the
number of signatures required to place an item on the local ballot from 2 to 8
percent of registered voters. Mayor Daniel Lurie, a Democrat, sponsored the
proposal, saying he wanted to simplify city ballots. As of Thursday, Measure D
[leads by a large
margin](https://www.sfelections.org/results/20261103w/index.html) of 15
percentage points.

### **Idaho**

In Idaho, Republican legislators took a different approach by trying to limit
initiatives on only one particular issue.

The proposal, HJR 4, would have [preemptively banned
initiatives](https://idahocapitalsun.com/2026/10/06/passing-hjr-4-would-give-
idaho-legislature-sole-authority-to-legalize-marijuana-other-drugs/) from
being used to legalize marijuana or other controlled substances. Voters
rejected the measure 66 to 34 percent.  

Idaho Republicans have intensified their efforts to limit citizen initiatives
since a [2018 campaign successfully expanded access to
Medicaid](https://ballotpedia.org/Idaho_Proposition_2,_Medicaid_Expansion_Initiative_\(2018\)),
according to Luke Mayville, executive director of Reclaim Idaho, the
organization that spearheaded the initiative.

Republicans in 2021 adopted [new rules for qualifying popular
initiatives](https://idahocapitalsun.com/2021/04/17/idaho-governor-signs-into-
law-legislation-to-raise-bar-on-ballot-initiatives/) that required petitions
to gather signatures from 6 percent of registered voters in all 35 legislative
districts. The rule would have effectively killed the initiative process,
Mayville told _Bolts,_ as a campaign would fail if it didn’t collect enough
petitions in any one of the many remote, sparsely populated regions of Idaho**
_._**

Reclaim Idaho sued, and the state supreme court unanimously struck down the
law and held that the state constitution protects a fundamental right to
initiative powers that legislators cannot interfere with. That meant lawmakers
would need to go down the route of a constitutional amendment to chip away at
direct democracy—as they tried on Tuesday. “That explains why we're in this
strange situation as voters of being asked to surrender our own rights,”
Mayville said.

![](https://boltsmag.org/wp-content/uploads/2023/08/Mayville.png)Luke Mayville
speaks at an event on behalf of an initiative supporting public school funding
that Reclaim Idaho tried to put on the ballot in 2022. (Photo by Chelsea
Harada, courtesy of Mayville)

Opponents of HJR 4 argued that the measure wasn't really about marijuana, and
that the reform would set a precedent for lawmakers to exempt other issues
from popular initiatives.

“We have every reason to think that if they can successfully convince voters
to surrender their power on one topic, they would come back again in future
cycles for other topics,” he told _Bolts_. “Many of the same legislators who
would prefer to take away citizens' ability to weigh in on drug policy would
also prefer to take away their ability to weigh in on taxation or education,
or any type of workers' rights policy.”

  
_This article has been updated after the Associated Press formally called the
defeat of Proposition 43 to reflect the final result in all seven states._
